chapters.n: The book opens by naming its source: this message came from the Lord to a prophet named Joel. We know almost nothing else about him, and scholars disagree about exactly when he lived.

f.g: His name means “Jehovah is God.”

chapters.n: Joel calls on the oldest people in the land to remember: has anything like this disaster ever happened before? The answer is no — this is unheard of.

f.g: Or “elders” — the senior leaders whose memories reached furthest back.

chapters.n: This catastrophe is so great it must be told to children and grandchildren for generations. Joel wants its lesson about turning to God passed down.
Wave after wave of locusts has stripped the land. Whatever one swarm left, the next devoured, until nothing remained. The four names may describe different kinds or growth stages of locusts.

f.g: The four Hebrew words (gazam, arbeh, yeleq, ḥasil) are all names for locusts, perhaps at different stages of life.

chapters.n: Those who live for drink are told to wake up and weep, because the vines are gone and there will be no new wine. Joel uses the disaster to shake people out of careless living.

f.g: Fresh grape juice just pressed from the harvest.

chapters.n: The locusts are pictured as an invading nation — countless and powerful, with teeth like a lion’s. Something small becomes terrifying when it comes in overwhelming numbers.

f.g: The Lord speaks of Israel as His own land.
Molars or jaw teeth — grinding teeth that chew everything.

chapters.n: The locusts have stripped the vines and gnawed the bark off the fig trees, leaving the branches bare and white. The vine and fig tree were symbols of Israel’s peace and prosperity.

f.g: Stripped the bark from.

chapters.n: The land should mourn like a young bride whose husband has died. Sackcloth was rough goat-hair cloth worn as a sign of grief.

f.g: Here a young woman betrothed or newly married; her loss is especially bitter.
Coarse, dark cloth worn in mourning or repentance.

chapters.n: With crops gone, there is nothing to offer at the temple. Even the daily worship is interrupted, and the priests grieve because they cannot perform their service.

f.g: “Meat” in KJV means food; this is the grain (flour) offering.

chapters.n: The three staple crops of the land — grain, wine, and olive oil — have all failed. Even the land itself seems to mourn.

f.g: KJV “corn” means grain, such as wheat or barley — not American maize.
Withers; grows weak.

chapters.n: Farmers and vineyard workers are told to wail because the whole harvest is lost. Their hard work has come to nothing.

f.g: Farmers; those who till the ground.

chapters.n: Every fruit tree has withered — and with them people’s joy. Joel links the outward drought to an inward emptiness among the people.

f.g: The Hebrew tappuaḥ may mean apple, apricot, or quince.

chapters.n: Joel turns to the priests and urges them to put on sackcloth and spend the night in mourning prayer. Spiritual leaders should lead the way in repentance.

f.g: Put on (sackcloth) — tie it around the waist.

chapters.n: Here is the remedy: call a holy fast, gather everyone to the temple, and cry to the Lord. When disaster strikes, God’s people turn to Him together.

f.g: A sacred gathering of the whole community for worship and prayer.

chapters.n: The locust plague is a warning sign of something bigger: “the day of the Lord,” a time when God steps in to judge. This phrase is a major theme of Joel’s book.

f.g: Hebrew Shaddai; there is a wordplay: “destruction” (shod) from “the Almighty” (Shaddai).

chapters.n: Joel points to what everyone can see: the food is gone, and the joyful feasts at the temple have stopped.

f.g: Food.

chapters.n: Seeds have shriveled in the dry ground, and storehouses stand empty and broken because there is nothing to put in them.

f.g: Granaries; storehouses for grain.
Lumps of dry earth.

chapters.n: Even the animals suffer. Herds wander confused, and flocks starve without pasture. The whole creation feels the effects of the disaster.

f.g: Wandering in confusion.

chapters.n: Joel himself prays, setting an example. Drought and heat have scorched the land as if it had been burned by fire.

f.w: O LORD, to thee will I cry

chapters.n: Even the wild animals seem to look to God, panting for water because the streams have dried up. If animals cry to God, how much more should His people?
Sound the alarm! Joel calls for the trumpet to warn the people in Jerusalem that the day of the Lord is coming. A trumpet blast was the ancient warning signal of approaching danger.

f.g: Hebrew shofar — a ram’s horn used for alarms and sacred gatherings.
Mount Zion, where the temple stood in Jerusalem.

chapters.n: That day will be dark and gloomy. A vast, powerful army will spread over the mountains like the dawn — unlike anything before or after. The locusts now foreshadow a greater, final judgment.

f.w: A day of darkness and of gloominess

chapters.n: This army devours everything like fire. Before it the land is lush like Eden; behind it, only wasteland. The image reverses the creation story.
They look like horses and charge like cavalry. A locust’s head really does resemble a small horse’s head.
Their noise is like rumbling chariots and crackling fire in dry stubble — an army lined up for battle.

f.g: Dry stalks left in a field after harvest; it burns fast.

chapters.n: People are terrified when they see this army coming; their faces turn pale with fear.

f.g: Probably “grow pale” or “lose their color” with fear.

chapters.n: The army is disciplined. Each soldier stays in line, climbing walls and marching without breaking ranks.

f.g: Swerve from their path.

chapters.n: No one pushes another; they cannot be stopped even by weapons. Swarming locusts were nearly impossible to fight.

f.g: Push or crowd.

chapters.n: They pour through the city, over walls and houses, and in through windows like thieves. Nowhere is safe from them.
Earth and heaven shake; sun, moon, and stars go dark. These cosmic signs show that this is God’s great day.

f.w: the sun and the moon shall be dark

chapters.n: The surprise: the Lord Himself leads this army. It carries out His word. Joel asks, “Who can endure that day?”
Yet it is not too late! The Lord pleads, “Turn to me with all your heart.” Even in judgment, God’s deepest desire is for His people to come back to Him.

f.w: turn ye even to me with all your heart

chapters.n: Real repentance is inward. Tearing clothes was a sign of grief, but God wants a broken heart, not a show. He is gracious, merciful, and ready to hold back punishment.

f.w: rend your heart, and not your garments
gracious and merciful, slow to anger

f.g: Relents from sending the disaster.

chapters.n: Who knows? Perhaps the Lord will turn and leave a blessing — even enough harvest to offer at the temple again. Joel does not presume, but he hopes.
Joel repeats the call: sound the trumpet, but this time to gather for a holy fast rather than to sound alarm.
Everyone must come — elders, children, even nursing babies and newlyweds who were normally excused from duties. Repentance is for the whole community.

f.g: Private room; bridal chamber.

chapters.n: The priests stand between the temple porch and the altar and plead: spare your people, so the nations cannot mock and ask, “Where is their God?”

f.w: between the porch and the altar
f.g: The courtyard area just in front of the temple building, where priests ministered.

chapters.n: The turning point of the book: the Lord responds with zeal and compassion for His land and people.

f.g: Zealous, deeply protective of what is His.

chapters.n: God promises to restore food — grain, wine, and oil — so they will be satisfied and no longer be laughed at by other nations.
The “northern army” will be driven away into the desert, with its front in the Dead Sea and its back in the Mediterranean, and its rotting stench will rise. Locust swarms often died in the sea.

f.g: The Dead Sea.
The western sea — the Mediterranean.

chapters.n: The land, which had “mourned,” is now told to rejoice, for the Lord, not the locusts, will do great things.
Even the animals can stop fearing; pastures are green again and trees bear fruit. Joel reverses each loss described in chapter 1.

f.w: the fig tree and the vine

chapters.n: Rain will come in its seasons. In Israel the “former” rains of autumn soften the soil for planting, and the “latter” rains of spring ripen the crops.

f.g: Some translate “the teacher of righteousness” — the Hebrew moreh can mean both “early rain” and “teacher.”

chapters.n: Threshing floors will be heaped with grain, and the vats will overflow with wine and oil — abundance replacing famine.

f.g: Vats — the troughs that catch juice from a winepress.
Threshing floors, where grain was separated from chaff.

chapters.n: One of the Bible’s most tender promises: God will restore the years the locusts devoured. He can redeem lost time and heal what was ruined.

f.w: I will restore to you the years
f.g: Many find personal hope here: the Lord can make up for losses — even those caused by sin — when we turn to Him.

chapters.n: The people will eat their fill and praise the God who acted with wonders. Their shame will be removed for good.
The greatest gift is not food but God’s presence: they will know He dwells among Israel and that there is no other God.

f.w: I am in the midst of Israel

chapters.n: A famous promise: God will pour out His Spirit on all kinds of people, and they will prophesy, dream, and see visions. Peter quoted this at Pentecost, and Moroni told Joseph Smith it was soon to be fulfilled.

f.w: I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh
your sons and your daughters shall prophesy

chapters.n: Even servants — men and women of the lowest social rank — will receive the Spirit. God’s gifts are not limited by class or gender.

f.g: Female servants.

chapters.n: God will show signs in heaven and on earth: blood, fire, and columns of smoke, signaling that His great day is near.
The sun will go dark and the moon turn red as blood before the Lord’s great day. Latter-day Saints see this among the signs preceding the Second Coming.
Whoever calls on the Lord’s name will be saved. Deliverance will be found in Zion and Jerusalem. Paul applied this to calling on Jesus Christ.

f.w: whosoever shall call on the name of the LORD shall be delivered
in mount Zion and in Jerusalem shall be deliverance

chapters.n: Joel looks to the future “in those days,” when the Lord gathers back His scattered people of Judah and Jerusalem. This connects to the latter-day gathering of Israel.

f.g: Restore the fortunes of; bring back the exiles.

chapters.n: The Lord will gather the nations to the valley of Jehoshaphat and judge them for scattering Israel and dividing His land.

f.g: The name means “Jehovah judges.” Tradition places it in the Kidron Valley next to Jerusalem.
Enter into judgment with them, as in a court case.

chapters.n: The nations treated God’s people as cheap goods, gambling for them and trading children for a prostitute or a drink. God sees every injustice done to the vulnerable.
The Lord addresses the coastal cities. Do they think they can pay Him back for something? Whatever harm they intend will quickly fall on their own heads.

f.g: Phoenician trading cities on the coast north of Israel, in modern Lebanon.
Philistia — the land of the Philistines on the southwest coast.

chapters.n: They looted the Lord’s silver and gold and the treasures of His temple and put them in their own temples.

f.g: Precious, desirable treasures.

chapters.n: Worse, they sold people of Judah as slaves to the Greeks, far from their homeland. Slave trading through Phoenician ports was well known in the ancient world.

f.g: Hebrew Yevanim — Ionians, Greeks living around the Aegean Sea.

chapters.n: God promises to bring the enslaved back from wherever they were sold, and to repay their captors.
Justice will be reversed: the slave traders’ own children will be sold, and sent to the Sabeans in distant Arabia.

f.g: People of Sheba in southern Arabia, famous long-distance traders.

chapters.n: Now the Lord issues a challenge to the nations: Prepare for war! Gather your strongest soldiers! This is an ironic summons to a battle they cannot win.

f.g: Literally “sanctify war” — ancient armies performed rituals before battle.

chapters.n: Joel turns a famous peace promise upside down: turn farm tools into weapons. Even weaklings should claim to be strong. (Isaiah and Micah foresee the opposite in the Messiah’s reign.)
The nations are told to assemble, and Joel prays for the Lord to bring down His own mighty ones — His heavenly armies.

f.g: The Lord’s warriors — likely His angelic hosts.

chapters.n: The nations come to the valley of Jehoshaphat, and the Lord sits as Judge. The battlefield becomes a courtroom.

f.w: there will I sit to judge

chapters.n: Harvest images describe judgment: swing the sickle, for the crop is ripe; tread the grapes, for the winepress overflows — their wickedness is full.

f.w: Put ye in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe

chapters.n: Huge crowds fill “the valley of decision” — the place where the Lord delivers His verdict. The day of the Lord is near.

f.g: The Hebrew suggests a verdict or sharp cutting — God’s decision, not man’s.

chapters.n: Sun, moon, and stars go dark — the same cosmic signs from chapter 2, showing this is the great day of the Lord.

f.w: The sun and the moon shall be darkened

chapters.n: The Lord roars like a lion from Zion and shakes heaven and earth. Yet for His own people He is a refuge and strength.

f.g: Literally “a refuge” or “shelter.”

chapters.n: Then everyone will know that the Lord lives in Zion. Jerusalem will be holy, and no foreign invader will pass through it again.
A picture of paradise: mountains drip with wine, hills flow with milk, and a fountain springs from the temple to water the dry valley. Ezekiel saw a similar river from the temple.

f.w: a fountain shall come forth of the house of the LORD

f.g: “Valley of acacias” — a dry valley, perhaps toward the Dead Sea.

chapters.n: Egypt and Edom, longtime enemies who shed innocent blood in Judah, will become wastelands.
In contrast, Judah and Jerusalem will be inhabited forever — a promise of lasting security for God’s people.
The book ends with cleansing and presence: the Lord will purify His people and dwell in Zion. God with His people is the final hope.

f.g: The Hebrew may mean God will avenge their blood or will declare them innocent; either way, He sets things right.
